blocks.label: THE CENTRAL IDEA
blocks.body: This is a picture of how your wellbeing is arranged right now. It is a season, not a personality type, and not a verdict. A future reflection may read differently, because your life can.

items.title: Your whole picture
items.body: Nine areas are read together, so one strong part of your life never erases a difficult stretch, and a difficult stretch never hides behind a capable exterior.

items.title: What moves together
items.body: Some areas rise and fall in each other's company. Noticing which travel together shows where a small effort reaches furthest.

items.title: The texture of your days
items.body: Your rhythm, your stress pattern, where tension settles, and how the short exercises felt all add colour to the picture.

items.title: A right sized next step
items.body: Suggestions are matched to the area asking for care, what gets in your way, the support you prefer, and how much plan fits your life this month.

items.label: WHAT IT CAN SAY, AND WHAT IT CANNOT
items.body: It can say how your wellbeing feels arranged today, which areas appear to travel together, and which small change is most likely to be worth your effort. It cannot say what caused what, how you will feel next month, or anything medical. Where it is confident, it speaks plainly. Where it is less certain, it says so rather than pretending.

items.label: A NOTE ON COMPARISON
items.body: You will not find yourself ranked against other people here. Comparison tends to produce anxiety rather than insight, and the honest answer to how do I compare needs far more than one reflection can gather. This report compares you only to yourself, and invites you to do the same when you retake it.

pages.title: The four words this report uses
pages.deck: Every area of your life is described with one of four words. They are deliberately broad, and they are the same four words wherever they appear in this report.

items.gloss: This area needs the gentlest care right now. Reserve is thin, and effort here costs more than it should.
Stretched, and asking for attention. Still functioning, but with less give than it used to have.
Holding reliably, without strain. Not remarkable, and not asking anything of you this month.
A real strength, and a place to stand. Something to spend deliberately, not simply admire.

blocks.label: WHY FOUR WORDS INSTEAD OF A SCORE
blocks.body: One sitting places you honestly inside a broad range, and that is what this report can give you truthfully. A number would suggest a precision no single reflection carries, and it would invite you to grade yourself rather than understand yourself. Words also travel better. Running on empty tells you what to do next. A number does not.

blocks.label: WHAT YOUR RHYTHM AND YOUR PRESSURE TOGETHER ARE SAYING
blocks.body: Your energy is not uniformly low. It moves through the day and lifts again late, and your pressure tends to lift alongside it. That combination is what makes stopping feel strangely effortful: the body is tired, and the day has not fully released you. Evenings then risk becoming a second working day of planning, scrolling or problem solving, at the hour you most need a softer landing.

pages.title: Your calm, body, and energy
pages.deck: The three areas closest to where you are being asked to begin, described together because, in this season, they move together.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Life has felt genuinely manageable, and your mind has been settling well once the day is done. That is a real form of wealth.

paras.label: How to spend it.
paras.text: Emotional steadiness makes you a safe harbour, for yourself and for the people around you. It is a strength worth using deliberately rather than just enjoying.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Calm rests on the conditions that produce it. When routines change, rebuild the settling habits early rather than assuming the calm will carry itself.

blocks.name: Body & recovery
blocks.stance: Offered as a reading to test against your experience

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Your body is genuinely resourced right now. Rest restores you, and there is reserve available when the day asks for more.

paras.label: How to spend it.
paras.text: Physical reserve is a resource the rest of your life can draw on. It is what makes harder conversations, bigger projects, and generous patience affordable.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Strength here is easy to take for granted. Keep the habits that built it visible, so a demanding stretch does not quietly dismantle them.

blocks.name: Usable energy
blocks.stance: Offered as a reading to test against your experience

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Energy is genuinely available to you, at the times you need it. That availability is doing quiet work across every other area of your life.

paras.label: How to spend it.
paras.text: Strong energy is a chance to invest rather than just cope. It is the season for the meaningful project, the deeper connection, the thing you have been deferring.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Keep respecting the recovery that funds this. Energy feels infinite until the week it is not, and the habits behind it deserve to survive your busiest month.

blocks.label: READING THESE THREE TOGETHER
blocks.body: Emotional calm can be described plainly because your answers there were clear and consistent. Body & recovery and Usable energy are offered a little more carefully, because they rest on a smaller set of questions. Where the picture is firm, this report says so. Where it is thinner, it says that too, and leaves you to decide whether it fits.

pages.title: Your meaning, agency, and relationships
pages.deck: The steadier areas carrying you through this season, and how to turn each one from comfort into structure.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Your work and your care for the people around you still connect to a reason larger than the task list. That coherence is why difficult days feel like part of something for you, rather than merely repetitive.

paras.label: The hidden cost.
paras.text: Meaning can make overextension feel noble. When purpose is strong, the body is often asked to subsidise commitments for longer than it can comfortably sustain. That is worth naming plainly, because it is the part most likely to go unnoticed.

paras.label: How to use this strength.
paras.text: Let your sense of meaning justify recovery as part of your contribution, rather than as time stolen from it. The question is not whether rest is deserved. It is which form of recovery protects the life you actually value.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Your actions have been landing. Intention travels to done with unusually little friction, and that reliability is a genuine asset.

paras.label: How to spend it.
paras.text: Strong agency can carry more than task lists. It is the muscle that protects boundaries, starts hard conversations, and changes systems rather than just surviving them.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Capability attracts load. The stronger this area, the more deliberately you need to choose what deserves it, or the strength becomes the reason for depletion elsewhere.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: You have trusted people with whom openness feels possible, and the way you described sharing agreed with that picture. Connection here reads as emotionally real rather than merely social on paper, which is a meaningful difference.

paras.label: How to use this strength.
paras.text: Ask your connections to protect what you are working on, not only to provide comfort afterwards. A simple boundary witnessed by someone close turns support into practical shelter.

paras.label: What not to assume.
paras.text: Strong relationships do not mean unlimited availability, yours or theirs. Protecting one evening from obligation can honour your connections better than staying reachable while exhausted.

blocks.label: YOUR STRENGTHS ARE THE PLAN, NOT THE BACKGROUND
blocks.body: It would be easy to read the stronger areas of this report as pleasant context and skip to the problems. That would be a mistake in your case. Meaning & direction, Agency & work, and Relationships & support are the resources that make any plan survivable. They protect your time, hold you accountable without shame, and supply the patience you will need on the days the plan does not go well. The suggestions ahead deliberately spend these strengths rather than leaving them idle.

pages.next: The quieter areas that decide what is realistic for you this month.

pages.title: Your money, growth, and surroundings
pages.deck: Three quieter areas that shape what is realistic for you, and what kind of support is likely to fit.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Money has been feeling steady to live with. Control is present, worry is low, and finances are funding life rather than dominating it.

paras.label: How to use this strength.
paras.text: Financial ease buys options: the unhurried decision, the genuinely restful break, the help that fits. Spend some of it on recovery without guilt.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Keep the habits that produced this ease boring and regular. Financial peace is quiet, and quiet things are easiest to stop tending.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Learning and growth are alive for you right now. New ideas are getting through, and you have been finding space to follow them.

paras.label: How to spend it.
paras.text: Curiosity this available is worth aiming at something. Let one thread of interest deepen rather than staying wide, and it will start paying the rest of your life back.

paras.label: What to protect.
paras.text: Protect the open space that makes this possible. Exploration is usually the first thing a crowded season deletes, and the deletion is rarely announced.

paras.label: What is working.
paras.text: Home and a familiar context give you genuine grounding. Your surroundings are not uniformly restorative, and the ground they give you is real and worth counting.

paras.label: How to use this strength.
paras.text: Place your first habit exactly at the boundary between your more demanding environment and your restorative one. The setting itself then becomes part of the cue, and you have to remember less.

paras.label: What this means for programs.
paras.text: Nearby, small group, culturally comfortable formats will suit you better than anonymous, high intensity experiences. Belonging should reduce the effort a program asks of you, never become another thing to adapt to.

blocks.label: HOW THESE THREE SET THE BOUNDARIES OF YOUR PLAN

items.text: Money says a paid option is possible, and never necessary.
Curiosity says keep the reading short and honestly interesting.
Belonging says stay close to familiar settings, in small groups.

blocks.first_move: Before stopping today, write tomorrow's open tasks on one small piece of paper and leave it where tomorrow will find it.

blocks.label: THE SHAPE OF THE RECOMMENDATION
blocks.body: Begin at the one place where your pressures, your pattern, and your day all meet. Keep the action small enough that a crowded day cannot defeat it. This plan is designed to survive your hardest ordinary day, not to impress your easiest one.

items.label: FIRST PRIORITY
items.title: Create one reliable seam
items.body: Give your day one repeatable cue it can learn to trust. The aim is not instant change. It is a recognisable transition your body can learn to expect.

items.label: SECOND PRIORITY
items.title: Watch one honest signal
items.body: Track only whether the thing this plan is aimed at feels slightly easier. That matters more than chasing a dramatic difference, and it is considerably harder to fake.

items.label: THIRD PRIORITY
items.title: Spend your strengths
items.body: Let what is strong in your life decide what can wait, and let one trusted person witness the experiment. Your strengths become the conditions for change rather than reasons to keep overextending.

items.label: YOUR PACING
items.title: Focused, not full
items.body: One anchor plus one optional support is enough. Everything else stays a saved option rather than an obligation.

blocks.label: WHAT IMPROVEMENT WOULD LOOK LIKE FOR YOU

items.text: The seam you chose feels more distinct from the rest of your day.
The thing you are caring for costs slightly less effort than it did.
Beginning is a little easier at the moment you choose to begin.
You can miss a day without the whole experiment turning into failure.

blocks.text: These are things to observe rather than outcomes you are being promised. If the pattern does not move over the next month, that is useful information, and your next reflection should revise the starting point rather than asking you to try harder at the same one.

blocks.label: WHY THIS PLAN IS SMALLER THAN YOU MIGHT EXPECT
blocks.body: Two things you told this reflection decided the size of this plan. Your current load is real, and your readings show a season with limited spare capacity. Under those conditions a large plan tends to fail in the first crowded week and leave you feeling worse than when you started, because now there is evidence. A small plan that survives contact with a real week is worth considerably more than an impressive one you abandon. If it feels almost too easy, it has been sized correctly.

pages.title: Your anchor practice
pages.deck: One practice, described properly. This is the single thing this report would ask you to keep if you kept nothing else.

cols.label: WHEN
cols.text: The last five minutes before you stop work, or before the evening's main task begins.

cols.label: WHAT YOU DO
cols.text: Write tomorrow's open tasks on one small piece of paper, then put it where tomorrow will find it. Close the notebook or the app afterwards.

cols.label: WHY IT IS THIS SMALL
cols.text: It takes minutes, uses paper you already have, and moves the mental juggling out of your head and onto a page that will hold it overnight.

items.title: The day is about to close
items.note: The pad is already where you stop

items.title: Leave it where tomorrow finds it

items.label: HOW TO SET IT UP TONIGHT
items.body: Put a pen and a small pad in the exact place your working day usually ends. Not a beautiful notebook, a working pad. Its only job is to be there when the day closes, so the practice never depends on finding materials.

items.label: WHAT IT SHOULD FEEL LIKE
items.body: Mildly relieving, and slightly mundane. The relief is the point: an open loop written down is a loop your mind no longer needs to rehearse. If it feels almost too simple to matter, it has been sized correctly.

items.label: PERMISSIONS, SO THIS STAYS GENTLE
items.body: The list does not need to be complete, ordered, or realistic. Three lines are plenty. If a day ends in chaos, one word on the page still counts. There is no correct format.

items.label: IF YOU FORGET, WHICH YOU WILL
items.body: Write it whenever you remember, even from bed. A late list still catches the loops. Missing a night changes nothing, and the list will be there for you the next evening either way.

pages.deck: One action a day, and deliberately nothing more. If a day is missed, the week is not.

rows.action: Put pen and pad where your day ends. Write tomorrow's list once.

items.label: WHAT COUNTS AS A GOOD WEEK
items.body: Four evenings with the loops on paper rather than in your head. An incomplete list still does the whole job.

items.label: WHAT WOULD BE TOO MUCH
items.body: Turning the list into a planning system, or ranking and re-ranking it until it becomes the evening's work.

blocks.label: WHY A LIST, RATHER THAN A RELAXATION PRACTICE
blocks.body: A scattered, foggy season seems to call for calm, and calm helps. But a mind juggling open loops cannot relax on command, because the juggling is doing a job: making sure nothing is dropped. Give the loops a page to live on and the mind can stand down honestly. The relaxation arrives as a consequence rather than a demand.

pages.title: Your optional supports
pages.deck: Small additions, chosen for your specific pattern. Take one at a time, and only after the anchor is steady. This is a shelf to choose from, not a list to complete.

items.title: Why transitions work better than commands
items.body: A short piece on why creating a boundary between effort and rest tends to work better than instructing yourself to relax.
items.why: Why this, for you. Your curiosity is available but your time is not, so this is deliberately four minutes rather than a course. Save it for day three, once the anchor itself is established. Understanding a practice after you have felt it tends to make it stick better than reading about it first.

items.title: A soft layered evening soundscape
items.body: Quiet, undemanding audio to sit alongside your anchor rather than replace it. Headphones optional.
items.why: Why this, for you. Your evenings have been carrying more activation than ease, and for some people a low, undemanding sound gives that motion something to settle against. Use it only if silence keeps your mind busy. If silence already works for you, skip this entirely.

items.title: Draw effort and ease as two lines
items.body: No artistic skill required. Sketch how each moved across your day, then circle one moment where the distance between them narrowed.
items.why: Why this, for you. Once this week is plenty. Your day has a shape worth seeing from the outside, and putting it on paper often makes it easier to work with than thinking about it. Treat it as noticing, not journalling.

items.title: A short unhurried walk
items.body: Ten minutes, no destination, no pace target. Outside if possible, near anything green if available.
items.why: Why this, for you. Your surroundings genuinely restore you, so this support borrows a strength you already have. It pairs well with the anchor on days when sitting still feels wrong.

blocks.body: The anchor alone is a complete plan. Every one of these is optional, and choosing none of them this month is a legitimate answer rather than a compromise.

items.title: For The Evening Climb
items.body: If you must work late, decide the stopping time before you begin rather than during. Deciding while tired reliably produces a later answer than deciding while fresh.

items.title: For The Dip In Your Day
items.body: Place your most demanding task where your energy naturally sits higher. Scheduling around your own rhythm costs nothing and saves real effort.

items.title: For The Role Switch
items.body: Change one physical thing when one part of your day ends. Shoes off, a different chair, a window opened. Transitions respond better to physical markers than to intentions.

items.title: For Crowded Weeks
items.body: Shrink rather than skip. The smallest version of the practice, on the way to the door if needed. The pattern is what you are protecting, not the duration.

blocks.body: Everything on this page is designed to cost you nothing extra. Not one of these adjustments asks for more time, only for a decision made earlier, or a small physical change at a moment that is already happening.

pages.title: The programs made for where you are

blocks.label: WHY A GUIDED PROGRAM TAKES YOU FURTHER

items.title: A setting that does some of the work
items.body: Spending around two hours a week in green surroundings is associated with good self reported health and wellbeing.

items.title: A protected room and a set time
items.body: Gentle, breath led movement is linked across review after review to lower perceived stress.

items.title: People beside you
items.body: Showing up alongside others has long been found to lighten the felt weight of a demanding season.

blocks.title: Nature immersion morning walks
blocks.what: Guided, unhurried group walks in green surroundings, early in the day. More noticing than exercising, with no pace requirements.
blocks.why: Green surroundings are among the most reliably supportive settings there are, and a scheduled group walk protects the time in a way good intentions rarely do. It suits a pattern that responds to place rather than to effort.
blocks.walkaway: A standing morning that belongs to you. Spending around two hours a week in nature is associated with good self reported health and wellbeing.

blocks.title: Restorative movement and deep rest day
blocks.what: A half day experience with unhurried mobility, guided rest, and quiet breaks. No intensive physical demand, and no overnight commitment.
blocks.why: It is gentle rather than challenging, which is exactly right while stopping is not yet fully restorative for you. It gives your body a longer experience of genuine rest without asking you to perform. Pair it with the series, or take it as your reset.
blocks.walkaway: A full day where rest is the whole point, of the kind that in trials with adults running low increased energy and reduced fatigue.

blocks.label: GOOD TO KNOW
blocks.body: Both programs are close to home, in small culturally comfortable groups, the format this report shows fits you best. Small guided connection circle joins the same shelf whenever your circumstances open it up.

blocks.label: TAKE YOUR PLACE
blocks.body: These programs are the closest match to the pattern this reflection found, chosen for your time, your setting and the exact thing you are working on. Small group places fill quickly, and the sooner you begin, the sooner your pattern can begin to change. Reserve your place, bring the practice you have already started, and let the room do the rest.

pages.next: How to find out whether any of this is true for you, over thirty days.

pages.title: A thirty day experiment
pages.deck: The purpose is to learn something about your own life, not to complete a perfect routine. One repeated cue becomes the spine. Everything else stays optional.

items.label: WEEK ONE
items.title: Build the cue
items.body: Use your anchor on at least three days. Record only whether it felt easier, the same, or harder. Three honest days are worth more than seven forced ones.

items.label: WEEK TWO
items.title: Protect one boundary
items.body: Choose one boundary that serves the anchor and let a trusted person know. Keep the cue even when the boundary slips. The cue is the experiment. The rest is just weather.

items.label: WEEK THREE
items.title: Add one gentle support
items.body: Choose one optional support, whichever made things simpler in week one. Add only that one. Subtraction is always allowed.

items.label: WEEK FOUR
items.title: Retake and choose
items.body: Repeat the reflection. Continue the free supports, consider a suitable program, or revise the starting point if the pattern did not move. All of these are useful outcomes.

blocks.title: WHAT TO NOTICE, IN FOUR MOMENTS
rows: After the anchor
How did it feel?
Easier, same, or harder
Tests the core idea directly
Next morning
How restored do you feel?
More, unchanged, or less
Tracks recovery rather than perfection
First demanding task
How hard was it to begin?
Easier, same, or harder
Tracks usable energy where it counts
End of the week
Did the plan fit real life?
Fit, partly, or did not fit
Separates whether it works from whether it is doable

blocks.label: WHEN TO REFLECT AGAIN
blocks.body: A short check after seven days, and the complete reflection after thirty days or after a program. When you compare, look at direction and lived experience rather than small differences. Your before and after pair is what turns this report from a snapshot into a story about your own year.

blocks.label: QUESTIONS WORTH CARRYING

items.text: What changes when your day has a clear seam in it, even if the workload does not?
Which of your strengths best protects this experiment without becoming another demand?
What is the smallest form of enough you can recognise in a real week?

blocks.label: ON THE DAYS IT DOES NOT GO WELL
blocks.body: You will miss days. That is expected, and it is built into the design of this plan rather than being a failure of it. A missed day tells you something about fit, which is genuinely useful information. If several days slip, the right response is to make the practice smaller rather than to try harder, and certainly rather than to think less of yourself. The plan should shrink before self judgement grows.

pages.next: What stands behind everything you have just read.

pages.title: What stands behind this report
pages.deck: A report that asks for your trust should be equally clear about where it is confident, where it is not, and what happens to what you shared.

items.label: HOW YOUR READING WAS FORMED
items.body: Each of the nine areas is read using established wellbeing questionnaires that have been tested and used in published research. They ask about how life feels rather than screening for any condition, and your answers were translated into the four broad words used throughout this report. The specific measures behind each area are listed in the appendix.

items.label: WHAT THE SHORT EXERCISES ADDED
items.body: The brief interactive moments, such as the breathing minute and the body map, add texture to the picture. They are sensitive to the kind of day you were having, so they are used to deepen or question what your answers already suggested. They are never used on their own to raise a concern.

items.label: HOW YOUR LIFE SHAPED THE SUGGESTIONS
items.body: What you told this reflection about your roles, your priorities, what gets in your way, and what you have already tried shaped the words in this report and the suggestions in it. Your circumstances change what is recommended to you. They never change how any area was read.

items.label: WHERE THIS REPORT SPEAKS CAREFULLY
items.body: Most of your areas rest on a full set of questions and are described plainly. Body & recovery and Usable energy rest on fewer questions, so they are offered for you to test rather than asserted. That difference in wording is deliberate, and it is worth trusting when you read it.

blocks.label: YOUR PRIVACY
blocks.body: This report belongs to you. Your individual answers, your readings, and your suggestions are never shared with an employer, and there is no route in the system for that to happen. Where organisations receive anything at all, it is combined across many people, with small groups withheld entirely so that no individual can be identified. Your name and identifying details are kept out of any pattern the system learns from. Nothing is collected that this reflection does not need.

blocks.label: THE LIMITS OF A SINGLE REFLECTION

items.text: One sitting reflects one day. This report describes how things feel now. It cannot establish what caused what, and a different week might read differently.
The short exercises are not tests. They are not measures of ability, intelligence, or health, and nothing in them is a medical reading.
Program suggestions describe fit. They match your pattern to a design. They are not predictions of benefit, and no outcome is promised anywhere in this report.
This is not care. If something feels persistently heavy, unsafe, painful, or hard to manage, speaking with someone you trust or a qualified professional is a real and worthwhile step.

blocks.text: The point of this report is not to explain you completely. It is to give you a truer place to begin.

blocks.text: These measures were chosen because they are published, widely used, and freely available, and because they ask about wellbeing rather than screening for illness. Their wording is never altered. Research practice treats short measures like these as indicating a broad range rather than a precise value, which is why this report speaks in four broad words rather than scores.

blocks.label: THE RESEARCH BEHIND THE CONNECTIONS DESCRIBED IN YOUR REPORT
blocks.body: The idea that effort carries a cost into the next day unless recovery follows it comes from research on work and recovery (Meijman and Mulder, 1998). The observation that strain in one area of life tends to spread into neighbouring areas, while intact strengths slow that spread, comes from work on personal resources (Hobfoll, 1989). Difficulty mentally switching off is one of the most consistently studied patterns in this field, and is associated with poorer rest and lower next morning energy across many studies (Sonnentag and Fritz, 2007; 2015). The reason your report treats the short interactive exercises as texture rather than evidence is that single session tasks are known to be informative about a day and unreliable about a person (Hedge, Powell and Sumner, 2018).

pages.next: The research behind your practices and the programs suggested to you.

pages.title: The research behind what was suggested
pages.deck: Every practice and program in this report was chosen for a reason that can be named and checked. Here are those reasons in full.

blocks.label: BEHIND YOUR SUGGESTED PRACTICES
blocks.body: Practices tied to a specific cue, in the form of after one thing I do another, are consistently more likely to be carried out than intentions alone (Gollwitzer, 1999; Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006). Habits form through repetition in a stable setting, and in the best known field study a single missed day made no measurable difference to that process (Lally et al., 2010), which is why this report treats missed days as ordinary. Briefly writing down tomorrow's open tasks before bed helped people settle faster in a controlled study (Scullin et al., 2018). Deliberate boundaries between work and home are associated with easier evening disengagement (Ashforth et al., 2000; Kreiner et al., 2009). Responding to lapses with self kindness rather than self criticism predicts returning to a practice sooner (Neff, 2003). Calm listening is associated with lower self reported stress (de Witte et al., 2020). Brief drawing offers a short term mood lift, working as gentle distraction (Drake and Winner, 2012). Gentle movement and time outdoors are associated with increased feelings of energy (Puetz et al., 2008) and restored attention (Kaplan, 1995). Brief views of greenery are associated with restored attention (Lee et al., 2015; Kaplan, 1995).

blocks.label: BEHIND THE PROGRAMS SUGGESTED TO YOU
blocks.body: Spending around two hours a week in nature is associated with good self reported health and wellbeing (White et al., 2019). Reviews of gentle, breath led movement report lower perceived stress across studies (Sharma, 2014). For low energy seasons, a randomised trial found low intensity activity increased energy and reduced fatigue (Puetz et al., 2008). Small group formats add the supportive presence of others, which is associated with buffering the felt weight of strain (Cohen and Wills, 1985), and social connection is consistently associated with wellbeing (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010).

blocks.label: HOW TO READ ANY OF THIS
blocks.body: Every study named here describes patterns across groups of people, which is the honest currency of wellbeing research. They are good reasons to expect that a practice or a program design is worth your time. They are not predictions about you specifically, and no finding here promises you a result. That distinction is the difference between evidence and marketing, and this report stays firmly on the evidence side of it.
